title: Hydration and Health: How Much Water Do You Really Need?

authorship.recommended_normalized_author: Healthy Weight Literacy Foundation Editorial Team

primary_question: How much water do I actually need to drink each day, and is the '8 glasses a day' rule real?
reader_intent: Get an accurate reference figure for daily water intake and understand why the 8x8 rule isn't evidence-based.
desired_reader_outcome: Reader knows the National Academies' Adequate Intake figures (3.7L men / 2.7L women, including food) and uses urine color as a practical adequacy check.

claims.proposition: The National Academies recommends approximately 3.7 liters (men) and 2.7 liters (women) of total water per day, including water from food (~19-20%).
claims.recommended_action: Matches claim-hydration-adequate-intake almost exactly (article says ~20% from food vs. the registry's verified ~19% — trivial rounding, not a material drift). The article does not formally cite NASEM in a Sources section despite naming them in prose.

internal_link_recommendations.reason: Both are foundational nutrition-basics content a new reader would want together.

disposition_reason: Accurate and already matches the registry's own verified hydration claim almost exactly, but this reader job is heavily duplicated by hydration-weight-health-daily-functioning (see cluster-hydration-duplicate) and lacks a formal Sources section despite naming NASEM in prose. Selected as the cluster survivor given its more focused, myth-debunking structure.
required_research: None — claim-hydration-adequate-intake already exists and supports this article directly.
recommended_rewrite_scope: Add a formal Sources section formally citing NASEM.
Incorporate the weight-management-specific angle (thirst-vs-hunger, water-before-meals) from the merged article during rewrite.
